original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، أَمَّا يَدُهُ إذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ فِيهَا نَجَاسَةٌ فَهِيَ كَسَائِرِ أَيْدِي الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَلَا يَضُرُّهَا تَلْوِيثُهَا بِالدَّمِ إذَا غَسَلَهَا كَمَا لَا يَضُرُّهَا تَلَوُّثُهَا بِالْخَبَثِ حَالَ الِاسْتِنْجَاءِ إذَا غَسَلَهَا بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ.
 وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ فِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ قَالَ:
 
{احْتَجَمَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَأَعْطَى الْحَجَّامَ أَجْرَهُ}
 وَلَوْ كَانَ سُحْتًا لَمْ يُعْطِهِ إيَّاهُ. وَفِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْ 
{أَنَسٍ - وَسُئِلَ عَنْ كَسْبِ الْحَجَّامِ -
 قَالَ:
 احْتَجَمَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ حَجَمَهُ أَبُو طِيبَةَ فَأَمَرَ لَهُ بِصَاعَيْنِ مِنْ طَعَامٍ وَكَلَّمَ أَهْلَهُ فَخَفَّفُوا عَنْهُ}
 وَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّ الْحَجَّامَ إذَا حَجَمَ يَسْتَحِقُّ أُجْرَةَ حَجْمِهِ عِنْدَ جَمَاهِيرِ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَإِنْ كَانَ فِيهِ قَوْلٌ ضَعِيفُ بِخِلَافِ ذَلِكَ. وَقَدْ أَرْخَصَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَهُ أَنْ يَعْلِفَهُ نَاضِحَهُ وَيُطْعِمَهُ رَقِيقَهُ كَمَا فِي حَدِيثِ 
{مُحْصَنٍ أَنَّ أَبَاهُ اسْتَأْذَنَ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي خَرَاجِ الْحَجَّامِ فَأَبَى أَنْ يَأْذَنَ لَهُ فَلَمْ يَزَلْ بِهِ حَتَّى قَالَ: أَطْعِمْهُ رَقِيقَك وَاعْلِفْهُ نَاضِحَك}
 رَوَاهُ أَبُو حَاتِمٍ ابْنُ حِبَّانَ فِي صَحِيحِهِ وَغَيْرُهُ. وَاحْتَجَّ بِهَذَا أَكْثَرُ الْعُلَمَاءِ أَنَّهُ لَا يَحْرُمُ. وَإِنَّمَا يُكْرَهُ لِلْحَرِّ تَنْزِيهًا.
 قَالُوا:
 لَوْ كَانَ حَرَامًا لَمَا أَمَرَهُ أَنْ يُطْعِمَهُ رَقِيقَهُ؛ لِأَنَّهُمْ مُتَعَبِّدُونَ
translated_text:
He replied:

Praise be to Allah. As for his hand, if there is no impurity on it, it is like the hands of other Muslims. Contact with blood does not affect its purity once he washes it, just as contact with filth while cleaning himself after relieving himself does not affect its purity if he washes it afterward.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that Ibn ʿAbbās said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, underwent cupping and paid the cupper his fee.”

Had it been unlawful gain, he would not have paid it to him. Also in the two Sahīh collections, Anas was asked about a cupper’s earnings and said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, underwent cupping. Abū Tībah performed it, and he ordered that he be given two sāʿ measures of food. He also spoke to his masters, who reduced the dues they required of him.”

There is no doubt that, according to the overwhelming majority of scholars, a cupper who performs cupping is entitled to his fee, although there is a weak opinion to the contrary. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, permitted him to use these earnings to feed his water-drawing camel and his slaves, as related in the hadith of Muhsan:

“His father asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for permission concerning income from cupping, but he refused to grant him permission. He persisted in asking until he said: ‘Use it to feed your slaves and your water-drawing camel.’”

Abū Hātim Ibn Hibbān narrated it in his Sahīh, as did others. Most scholars cited this as evidence that such earnings are not unlawful; for a free person, they are merely disliked, not prohibited. They argued that, had these earnings been unlawful, he would not have instructed him to use them to feed his slaves, since they too are bound by religious obligations.

original_text:
وَمِنْ الْمُحَالِ أَنْ يَأْذَنَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنْ يُطْعِمَ رَقِيقَهُ حَرَامًا.
 وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ قَالَ:
 بَلْ يَحْرُمُ؛ لِمَا رَوَى مُسْلِمٌ فِي صَحِيحِهِ عَنْ رَافِعِ بْنِ خَدِيجٍ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا -
 أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَالَ:
 
{كَسْبُ الْحَجَّامِ خَبِيثٌ وَثَمَنُ الْكَلْبِ خَبِيثٌ وَمَهْرُ الْبَغِيِّ خَبِيثٌ}
 
" وَفِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْ 
{ابْنِ أَبِي جحيفة قَالَ: رَأَيْت أَبِي اشْتَرَى حَجَّامًا فَأَمَرَ بِمَحَاجِمِهِ فَكُسِرَتْ فَسَأَلْته عَنْ ذَلِكَ؟
 فَقَالَ:
 إنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ نَهَى عَنْ ثَمَنِ الدَّمِ}
 .
 قَالَ هَؤُلَاءِ:
 فَتَسْمِيَتُهُ خَبِيثًا يَقْتَضِي تَحْرِيمَهُ كَتَحْرِيمِ مَهْرِ الْبَغِيِّ وَحُلْوَانِ الْكَاهِنِ.
 قَالَ الْأَوَّلُونَ:
 قَدْ ثَبَتَ عَنْهُ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: "
 
{مَنْ أَكَلَ مِنْ هَذَيْنِ الشَّجَرَتَيْنِ الْخَبِيثَتَيْنِ فَلَا يَقْرَبَن مَسْجِدَنَا}
 
" فَسَمَّاهُمَا خَبِيثَتَيْنِ بِخُبْثِ رِيحِهِمَا وَلَيْسَتَا حَرَامًا.
 وَقَالَ:
 "
 
{لَا يُصَلِّيَن أَحَدُكُمْ وَهُوَ يُدَافِعُ الْأَخْبَثِينَ}
 أَيْ: الْبَوْلُ وَالْغَائِطُ. فَيَكُونُ تَسْمِيَتُهُ خَبِيثًا لِمُلَاقَاةِ صَاحِبِهِ النَّجَاسَةَ؛ لَا لِتَحْرِيمِهِ؛ بِدَلِيلِ أَنَّهُ أَعْطَى الْحَجَّامَ أَجْرَهُ وَأَذِنَ لَهُ أَنْ يُطْعِمَهُ الرَّقِيقَ وَالْبَهَائِمَ. وَمَهْرُ الْبَغِيِّ وَحُلْوَانُ الْكَاهِنِ لَا يَسْتَحِقُّهُ وَلَا يُطْعَمُ مِنْهُ رَقِيقٌ وَلَا بَهِيمَةٌ.
 وَبِكُلِّ حَالٍ فَحَالُ الْمُحْتَاجِ إلَيْهِ لَيْسَتْ كَحَالِ الْمُسْتَغْنِي عَنْهُ كَمَا قَالَ السَّلَفُ:
 كَسْبٌ فِيهِ بَعْضُ الدَّنَاءَةِ خَيْرٌ مِنْ مَسْأَلَةِ النَّاسِ.
 وَلِهَذَا لَمَّا تَنَازَعَ الْعُلَمَاءُ فِي أَخْذِ الْأُجْرَةِ عَلَى تَعْلِيمِ الْقُرْآنِ وَنَحْوِهِ:
translated_text:
and it is inconceivable that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would permit him to feed his slaves anything unlawful.

Others said that such earnings are indeed unlawful, citing what Muslim narrated in his Sahīh from Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj—may Allah be pleased with them both—that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A cupper’s earnings are foul, the price of a dog is foul, and a prostitute’s fee is foul.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn Abī Juhayfah said:

“I saw my father buy a slave who practised cupping. He ordered that his cupping instruments be broken, and they were broken. I asked him about this, and he said: ‘The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade the price of blood.’”

Those scholars said: Describing these earnings as foul implies that they are forbidden, just as a prostitute’s fee and a soothsayer’s fee are forbidden.

Those who held the first view replied: It is established that he said:

“Whoever eats from these two foul plants must not come near our mosque.”

He called them foul because of their offensive smell, yet they are not forbidden. He also said:

“Let none of you pray while holding back the two foul things”—that is, urine and feces.

Thus, describing these earnings as foul is due to the earner’s contact with impurity, not because they are forbidden. The evidence for this is that he paid the cupper his fee and permitted him to use it to feed slaves and animals. By contrast, neither a prostitute nor a soothsayer is entitled to such fees, nor may they be used to feed slaves or animals.

In any case, someone who needs these earnings is not in the same position as someone who can do without them. As the early generations said:

“Earnings that carry some indignity are better than begging from people.”

For this reason, when the scholars differed over accepting payment for teaching the Quran and similar activities:

original_text:
كَانَ فِيهِ ثَلَاثَةُ أَقْوَالٍ فِي مَذْهَبِ الْإِمَامِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِ:
 أَعْدَلُهَا أَنَّهُ يُبَاحُ لِلْمُحْتَاجِ قَالَ أَحْمَد: أُجْرَةُ التَّعْلِيمِ خَيْرٌ مِنْ جَوَائِزِ السُّلْطَانِ وَجَوَائِزُ السُّلْطَانِ خَيْرٌ مِنْ صِلَةِ الْإِخْوَانِ. وَأُصُولُ الشَّرِيعَةِ كُلُّهَا مَبْنِيَّةٌ عَلَى هَذَا الْأَصْلِ أَنَّهُ يُفَرَّقُ فِي الْمَنْهِيَّاتِ بَيْنَ الْمُحْتَاجِ وَغَيْرِهِ كَمَا فِي الْمَأْمُورَاتِ. وَلِهَذَا أُبِيحَتْ الْمُحَرَّمَاتُ عِنْدَ الضَّرُورَةِ لَا سِيَّمَا إذَا قُدِّرَ أَنَّهُ يَعْدِلُ عَنْ ذَلِكَ إلَى سُؤَالِ النَّاسِ. فَالْمَسْأَلَةُ أَشَدُّ تَحْرِيمًا؛
 وَلِهَذَا قَالَ الْعُلَمَاءُ:
 يَجِبُ أَدَاءُ الْوَاجِبَاتِ وَإِنْ لَمْ تَحْصُلْ إلَّا بِالشُّبُهَاتِ كَمَا ذَكَرَ أَبُو طَالِبٍ وَأَبُو حَامِدٍ: أَنَّ الْإِمَامَ أَحْمَد سَأَلَهُ رَجُلٌ قَالَ: إنَّ ابْنًا لِي مَاتَ وَعَلَيْهِ دَيْنٌ وَلَهُ دُيُونٌ أَكْرَهُ تَقَاضِيهَا.
 فَقَالَ لَهُ الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد:
 أَتَدَعُ ذِمَّةَ ابْنِك مُرْتَهِنَةً؟
 يَقُولُ:
 قَضَاءُ الدَّيْنِ وَاجِبٌ وَتَرْكُ الشُّبْهَةِ لِأَدَاءِ الْوَاجِبِ هُوَ الْمَأْمُورُ.
 وَلِهَذَا اتَّفَقَ الْعُلَمَاءُ عَلَى أَنَّهُ يُرْزَقُ الْحَاكِمُ وَأَمْثَالُهُ عِنْدَ الْحَاجَةِ وَتَنَازَعُوا فِي الرِّزْقِ عِنْدَ عَدَمِ الْحَاجَةِ وَأَصْلُ ذَلِكَ فِي كِتَابِ اللَّهِ فِي قَوْلِهِ فِي وَلِيِّ الْيَتِيمِ:
 
{وَمَنْ كَانَ غَنِيًّا فَلْيَسْتَعْفِفْ وَمَنْ كَانَ فَقِيرًا فَلْيَأْكُلْ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ}
 فَهَكَذَا يُقَالُ فِي نَظَائِرِ هَذَا؛ إذْ الشَّرِيعَةُ مَبْنَاهَا عَلَى تَحْصِيلِ الْمَصَالِحِ وَتَكْمِيلِهَا وَتَعْطِيلِ الْمَفَاسِدِ وَتَقْلِيلِهَا. وَالْوَرَعُ تَرْجِيحُ خَيْرِ الْخَيْرَيْنِ بِتَفْوِيتِ أَدْنَاهُمَا وَدَفْعِ شَرِّ الشَّرَّيْنِ وَإِنْ حَصَلَ أَدْنَاهُمَا. وَقَدْ جَاءَ فِي الْحِجَامَةِ أَحَادِيثُ كَثِيرَةٌ. وَفِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ
translated_text:
there were three views within the school of Imam Ahmad and among other scholars. The most balanced is that it is permissible for someone in need. Ahmad said: “Payment for teaching is better than grants from the ruler, and grants from the ruler are better than gifts from one’s brethren.”

All the principles of the Sharia rest on this foundation: a distinction is made between someone in need and someone who is not, regarding prohibitions just as regarding commands. Thus, prohibited things become permissible in cases of necessity, especially if the alternative would be to beg from people, for begging is more strictly prohibited.

For this reason, the scholars said that obligations must be fulfilled even if they can only be fulfilled through doubtful means. As Abū Tālib and Abū Hāmid related, a man asked Imam Ahmad: “A son of mine has died owing debts, and others owe him debts that I am reluctant to collect.”

Imam Ahmad said to him: “Will you leave your son bound by his unpaid debt?”

His point was that repaying a debt is obligatory, and one is commanded to set aside one’s misgivings in order to fulfil an obligation.

Likewise, the scholars agreed that a judge and others in comparable positions should receive a stipend when in need, though they differed over receiving one when there is no need. The basis for this is in the Book of Allah, in His words concerning an orphan’s guardian:

“Whoever is wealthy should refrain, and whoever is poor may take a reasonable amount.”

The same applies to comparable cases, for the Sharia is founded on securing and perfecting benefits, and eliminating and reducing harms. True scrupulousness means choosing the greater of two goods at the expense of the lesser, and averting the greater of two evils even if the lesser results.

Many hadiths have been reported concerning cupping. In the two Sahīh collections, it is reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

original_text:
أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{شِفَاءُ أُمَّتِي فِي ثَلَاثٍ: شَرْبَةُ عَسَلٍ أَوْ شَرْطَةُ مِحْجَمٍ. أَوْ كَيَّةُ نَارٍ وَمَا أُحِبُّ أَنْ أَكْتَوِيَ}
 وَالتَّدَاوِي بِالْحِجَامَةِ جَائِزٌ بِالسُّنَّةِ الْمُتَوَاتِرَةِ وَبِاتِّفَاقِ الْعُلَمَاءِ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ امْرَأَةٍ مُنْقَطِعَةٍ أَرْمَلَةٍ. وَلَهَا مَصَاغٌ قَلِيلٌ تَكْرِيهِ وَتَأْكُلُ كِرَاهُ. فَهَلْ هُوَ حَلَالٌ؟ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، هَذَا جَائِزٌ عِنْدَ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَغَيْرِهِمَا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ. وَقَدْ كَرِهَهُ مَالِكٍ وَأَحْمَد وَأَصْحَابُ مَالِكٍ وَكَثِيرٌ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد. وَهَذِهِ كَرَاهَةُ تَنْزِيهٍ لَا كَرَاهَةُ تَحْرِيمٍ. وَهَذَا إذَا كَانَتْ بِجِنْسِهِ وَأَمَّا بِغَيْرِ جِنْسِهِ فَلَا بَأْسَ. فَهَذِهِ الْمَرْأَةُ إذَا أَكْرَتْهُ وَأَكَلَتْ كِرَاهُ لِحَاجَتِهَا لَمْ تُنْهَ عَنْ ذَلِكَ؛ لَكِنْ عَلَيْهَا الزَّكَاةُ عِنْدَ أَكْثَرِ الْعُلَمَاءِ. كَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَمَالِكٍ وَالْإِمَامِ أَحْمَد. وَهَذَا إنْ أَكْرَتْهُ لِمَنْ تَزَّيَّنُ لِزَوْجِهَا أَوْ سَيِّدِهَا أَوْ لِمَنْ يَحْضُرُ بِهِ حُضُورًا مُبَاحًا مِثْلَ أَنْ يَحْضُرَ عُرْسًا يَجُوزُ حُضُورُهُ. فَأَمَّا إنْ أَكْرَتْهُ لِمَنْ تَزَّيَّنُ بِهِ لِلرِّجَالِ الْأَجَانِبِ فَهَذَا لَا يَجُوزُ.
translated_text:
that he said:

“Healing for my community lies in three things: a drink of honey, an incision with a cupping lancet, or cauterization with fire. But I do not like to undergo cauterization.”

Treatment by cupping is permissible according to the mass-transmitted Sunnah and the agreement of the scholars.

He was asked:

A widow left on her own has a small amount of jewellery which she hires out, supporting herself with the rent. Is this lawful or not?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. This is permissible according to Abū Hanīfa, al-Shāfi'ī and other scholars. Mālik, Ahmad, Mālik’s followers and many of Ahmad’s followers considered it disliked. This, however, means that it is discouraged, not forbidden. This applies when the rent is of the same kind as the jewellery; if it is of a different kind, there is no objection.

Thus, if this woman hires out her jewellery and supports herself with the rent because she is in need, she should not be forbidden from doing so. However, she must pay zakat on it according to most scholars, including Abū Hanīfa, Mālik and Imam Ahmad.

This applies if she hires it out to a woman who adorns herself for her husband or master, or to someone who wears it to a permissible gathering, such as a wedding that one may lawfully attend. But if she hires it out to a woman who adorns herself with it for men who are not her mahrams, this is not permissible.

original_text:
وَأَمَّا إنْ أَكْرَتْهُ لِمَنْ تَزَّيَّنُ بِهِ لِفِعْلِ الْفَاحِشَةِ فَهَذَا أَعْظَمُ مِنْ أَنْ تَسْأَلَ عَنْهُ.
 قَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَتَعَاوَنُوا عَلَى الْبِرِّ وَالتَّقْوَى وَلَا تَعَاوَنُوا عَلَى الْإِثْمِ وَالْعُدْوَانِ}
 . وَلَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُعَانَ أَحَدٌ عَلَى الْفَاحِشَةِ وَلَا غَيْرِهَا مِنْ الْمَعَاصِي؛ لَا بِحِلْيَةِ وَلَا لِبَاسٍ وَلَا مَسْكَنٍ وَلَا دَابَّةٍ وَلَا غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ؛ لَا بكرى وَلَا بِغَيْرِهِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ الشَّمَّاعِينَ الَّذِينَ يَكْرُونَ الشَّمْعَ. ثُمَّ إنَّهُمْ يَزِنُونَهُ. أَوَّلًا فَإِذَا رَجَعَ وَزَنُوهُ ثَانِيًا وَأَخَذُوا نَقْصَهُ. فَهَلْ يُكْرَهُ ذَلِكَ؟ وَإِذَا كُسِرَ الشَّمْعُ فَهَلْ يَلْزَمُ الَّذِي اكْتَرَاهُ؟ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
أَمَّا الشَّمْعُ إذَا أَعْطَاهُ لِمَنْ يُوقِدُهُ وَقَالَ:
 كُلَّمَا نَقَصَ مِنْهُ أُوقِيَّةٌ بِكَذَا فَإِنَّ هَذَا جَائِزٌ. وَلَيْسَ هَذَا مِنْ بَابِ الْإِجَارَاتِ وَلَا بَابِ الْبَيْعِ اللَّازِمِ؛ فَإِنَّ الْبَيْعَ اللَّازِمَ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَكُونَ الْمَبِيع فِيهِ مَعْلُومًا؛ بَلْ هَذَا مُعَاوَضَةٌ جَائِزَةٌ لَا لَازِمَةٌ.
 كَمَا لَوْ قَالَ:
 اُسْكُنْ فِي هَذِهِ الدَّارِ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ بِدِرْهَمِ وَلَمْ يُوَقِّتْ أَجَلًا فَإِنَّ هَذَا جَائِزٌ فِي أَظْهَرِ قَوْلَيْ الْعُلَمَاءِ. فَمَسْأَلَةُ الْأَعْيَانِ نَظِيرُ هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ فِي الْمَنَافِعِ وَهُوَ إذْنٌ فِي الْإِتْلَافِ
translated_text:
But if she hires it out to a woman who adorns herself with it in order to commit sexual immorality, this is too grave a matter even to ask about.

Allah Most High says:

“Cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression.”

It is not permissible to help anyone commit sexual immorality or any other sin, whether by providing jewellery, clothing, accommodation, a riding animal, or anything else, whether for hire or otherwise. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Candle sellers hire out candles, weighing them before handing them over, then weighing them again upon their return and charging for the loss in weight. Is this disliked? If a candle breaks, is the person who hired it liable or not?

He answered:

If someone gives candles to another person to burn, saying, “For every ūqiyya (a unit of weight) consumed, the charge is such-and-such,” this is permissible. It does not fall under lease contracts or binding sales, since a binding sale requires the goods being sold to be known. Rather, it is a revocable exchange, not a binding one.

This is like saying, “Live in this house for one dirham a day,” without specifying a term. This is permissible according to the stronger of the two scholarly opinions. Thus, this case involving tangible property is analogous to that case involving the use of property. It constitutes permission to consume the property

عَلَى وَجْهِ الِانْتِفَاعِ بِعَرْضِ كَمَا لَوْ قَالَ:

عَنْ زركشي اُسْتُعْمِلَ عِنْدَهُ مِنْدِيلٌ فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ أَذِنُوا لَهُ فِي غَسْلِهِ فَعَدَتْ عَلَيْهِ أَمَةُ الصَّانِعِ فِي صَقْلِ الذَّهَبِ فتقرض الْمِنْدِيلُ. فَهَلْ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ غَرَامَةُ الْمِنْدِيلِ؟

translated_text:
for beneficial use in return for consideration, as when someone says, “Throw your goods into the sea, and I will pay their value.” This is undoubtedly permissible, because the person undertaking payment benefits from lightening the load, just as he benefits by undertaking payment here. Thus, burning candles for a charge is permissible provided their consumption is known. However, they must be burned for a permissible purpose, not a prohibited one.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A zarkashī artisan was commissioned to make a cloth. When he had finished, its owners permitted him to wash it. However, the artisan’s slave woman mishandled it while polishing the goldwork, leaving cuts in the cloth. Must he compensate them for the cloth?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. If the slave woman damaged the cloth, the claim for compensation attaches to her person. Her owner must either pay compensation for the damage or surrender her so that compensation can be recovered from her value.

Whether the damage was caused by her, her master, or someone else, the person responsible is not liable for what the owners spent on the cloth. Its value is assessed without these cuts and again after they have occurred, and those responsible must compensate for the reduction in value. If they mutually agree that the artisan should take the cloth and pay them its market value before it was cut, that is permissible. He is not obliged to give them a new cloth better than it.

وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ إجَارَةِ الْجَوَامِيسِ يَسْتَأْجِرُهَا عَامًا وَاحِدًا مُطْلَقًا وَغَرَضُهُ لَبَنُهَا وَيَسْتَعْمِلُهَا لِذَلِكَ. وَإِنَّمَا جَعَلُوهُ مُطْلَقًا أَنَّهُ يَسْتَعْمِلُهَا وَالْقَصْدُ اللَّبَنُ. وَالْغَنَمُ أَيْضًا هَلْ تَجُوزُ إجَارَتُهَا لِلَّبَنِ؟ وَهَلْ يَجُوزُ أَنْ تُعْطَى لِمَنْ يَرْعَاهَا بِصُوفِهَا وَلَبَنِهَا؟ أَمْ لَا؟ .
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةُ فِيهَا نِزَاعٌ مَعْرُوفٌ بَيْنَ السَّلَفِ وَالْعُلَمَاءِ وَكَذَلِكَ فِي اشْتِرَاءِ اللَّبَنِ مُدَّةً مِقْدَارًا مُعَيَّنًا مِنْ ذَلِكَ اللَّبَنِ يَأْخُذُهُ أَقْسَاطًا مِنْ هَذِهِ الْمَاشِيَةِ. وَالْمَنْعُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ هُوَ الْمَعْرُوفُ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

About leasing buffaloes: someone leases them for one year on unrestricted terms, intending to obtain their milk, and uses them for that purpose. The lease is left unrestricted on the understanding that he will make use of them, though the milk is his aim. Is it also permissible to lease sheep for their milk? And is it permissible to entrust them to someone who will tend them in return for their wool and milk, or not?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. There is a well-known disagreement on this issue among the early generations and the scholars. The same applies to purchasing a specified quantity of milk over a period, to be received in instalments from these livestock. Prohibition is the well-known position in the schools of Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad.

These scholars said:

This is the sale of something neither seen nor described; indeed, it is the sale of something nonexistent that has not yet come into being. A lease concerns benefits, not tangible property, whereas these are tangible things.

These scholars also said:

Hiring a wet nurse to breastfeed is contrary to legal analogy but was permitted because of need. They disagreed about this hiring arrangement.

One view is:

The subject of the contract is her service, while breastfeeding is incidental to it. This is the view of Ibn ʿAqīl and others.

Another view is:

Rather,

 أَنَّ الْإِجَارَةَ الْمَسْئُولَ عَنْهَا جَائِزَة؛ فَإِنَّ الْأَدِلَّةَ الشَّرْعِيَّةَ الدَّالَّةَ عَلَى الْجَوَازِ بِعِوَضِهَا وَمُقَايَسَتِهَا تَتَنَاوَلُ هَذِهِ الْإِجَارَةَ وَلَيْسَ مِنْ الْأَدِلَّةِ مَا يَنْفِي ذَلِكَ؛

This rests on regarding it as a contract concerning tangible property, and contracts concerning tangible property fall under the category of sales. The disagreement here is terminological: this arrangement falls within the broad meaning of sale, which encompasses tangible property and benefits, whether already in existence or not. It does not fall within the narrower meaning of sale, which is confined to existing tangible property.

They likewise disagreed over advance-payment contracts: are they a form of sale? There are two views. Can an advance-payment contract be concluded using the word “sale”? There are two positions on this within the school of Ahmad and those of others. Some who did not classify it as a sale even said that an advance-payment contract providing for immediate delivery is permissible when concluded using the word “sale”, but not the word “salam”. The correct view is that contracts are judged by their substance, not merely their wording.

The correct position is that the lease asked about is permissible. The scriptural evidence establishing the permissibility of compensated transactions, together with the analogies drawn from it, encompasses this lease, and no evidence rules it out.

The Sunnah and the consensus of the Muslim community establish the permissibility of this arrangement. It would be contrary to legal analogy only if an analogy drawn from another scriptural text conflicted with it. Yet nothing in the other scriptural texts or the analogies drawn from them contradicts it.

The assertion that hiring and leasing concern only benefits, not tangible property, is not a statement of Allah, His Messenger, the Companions, or the leading scholars. It is merely a statement made by a group of people.

We therefore say to them: We do not concede that hiring and leasing can concern benefits alone. Rather, they may concern something that is continually produced and replenished while the underlying property remains, such as the water of a well and similar things, whether what is obtained is tangible property or a benefit. Likewise, property placed in an endowment may yield something that is renewed and produced successively, whether that yield is a benefit or tangible property, such as dates, milk, or spring water. The same applies to a gratuitous loan for use, where benefit is obtained from something continually produced and replenished.

Thus, one speaks of lending a mount to be ridden, granting the use of a date palm, or lending a she-camel for its milk. If someone lends another a she-camel to drink its milk and then return it, or grants him the use of a date palm to eat its fruit and then return it, this is like lending him a mount to ride and then return. He was asked:

A sick man asked someone to treat him and cover his expenses, and he did so. Is the person who paid entitled to demand reimbursement from the sick man?

He replied:

If he covered the expenses expecting reimbursement, whether expressly stipulated or understood by custom, he is entitled to demand reimbursement. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A blind man was made party to a written lease. Is his lease valid?

He replied:

A blind person’s renting and purchasing are valid according to the majority of scholars, including Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, and Imam Ahmad according to the well-known position reported from him. The item purchased or rented must be described to him. If he finds that it does not match the description, he has the right to rescind the contract.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man does not have enough to meet his needs and leads prayers for payment. Is this permissible or not?

He replied:

Hiring someone to lead prayers is not permissible according to the well-known position in the schools of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, and Imam Ahmad.

Another view permits it. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī, one view reported from Imam Ahmad, and an opinion within Mālik’s school. The same disagreement applies to giving the call to prayer. However, the well-known position in Mālik’s school permits hiring someone to give the call to prayer and to lead prayers in conjunction with that duty, but not to lead prayers alone.

A third view within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere concerning payment for these duties and similar activities, such as teaching, is that it is permissible when there is a need, but not otherwise. Allah knows best.

A man died, having stipulated in his will that someone be paid in dirhams to pray on his behalf. What is the ruling?

He replied:

No one may perform an obligatory prayer on another’s behalf, whether for payment or otherwise, by agreement of the imams. Indeed, they agree that it is not permissible to hire someone even to perform voluntary prayers on one’s behalf, whether during one’s lifetime or after one’s death. How much less permissible, then, is hiring someone to perform obligatory prayers on one’s behalf!

The scholars differed only over whether a deceased person benefits when someone performs voluntary prayers without payment and dedicates their reward to him. There are two scholarly views on this. Likewise, if the deceased had vowed to pray but died before fulfilling his vow, may those vowed prayers be performed on his behalf? There are two views, both reported from Imam Ahmad.

However, the dirhams he bequeathed should be given in charity on his behalf, specifically to those who pray, so that the deceased receives a reward. He will also have a share in the reward of every prayer they perform with the help of his charity, without their own reward being diminished in the least. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever provides a fasting person with food to break his fast will have a reward like his.”

And he said:

“Whoever equips a warrior has himself taken part in the campaign.”

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A scholar was approached by someone wishing to read to him some hadiths of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and other religious sciences, but he refused to teach them except for payment. He was told:

“The reports describing how the early generations and the imams of guidance taught knowledge solely for the sake of Allah, the Most Generous, are too well known to escape any reasonable person. Such conduct is inappropriate.”

He replied:

“Am I to teach without payment? That is forbidden for me!”

Is his statement correct or false? Is this an ignorant statement for which he may be excused? Is he permitted to accept payment for teaching beneficial knowledge, or is that disliked for him?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. Teaching the Quran and religious knowledge without payment is the finest of deeds and the most beloved to Allah. This is a self-evident teaching of Islam, not something unknown to anyone raised in Muslim lands. The Companions, the Followers, the generation after them, and other scholars renowned throughout the Muslim community for their knowledge of the Quran, hadith, and jurisprudence taught without payment. None of them taught for payment at all. For the scholars are the heirs of the prophets, and the prophets left neither dinars nor dirhams

but only knowledge; whoever acquires it has acquired an abundant share. The prophets—may Allah Most High be pleased with them all—taught knowledge without payment. As Noah, peace be upon him, said:

“I ask you no payment for it. My reward rests only with the Lord of all worlds.”

Hūd, Sālih, Shuʿayb, Lot, and others said the same. Likewise, the Seal of the Messengers said:

“Say, ‘I ask you no payment for it, nor am I one of the pretentious.’”

And he said:

“Say, ‘I ask you no payment for it—only that whoever wills should take a path to his Lord.’”

The scholars have never disputed that teaching the Quran, hadith, jurisprudence, and other such subjects without payment is a righteous deed, let alone that it is permissible. Indeed, it is a collective obligation. For teaching the knowledge he expounded is a collective obligation, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“Convey from me, even if only a single verse.”

And he said:

“Let those present convey it to those absent.”

This differs from someone who is financially self-sufficient: he has no need to earn a living, and thus no need prompting him to perform these duties for other than Allah. Rather, since Allah has provided him with sufficient means and this is a communal obligation, he is among those required to fulfil it. If it cannot be fulfilled except through him, it becomes an individual obligation upon him. And Allah knows best.

If someone rents a house for his own enjoyment, may he let it out?

He replied:

If someone hires a service for a prohibited act, such as singing, fornication, false testimony, or killing someone whose life is protected, that hiring is prohibited.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section: Hiring Someone to Provide a Prohibited Service

Hiring someone to provide a prohibited service—such as illicit sexual intercourse, sodomy, singing, transporting wine, or the like—is invalid. Yet if the hirer receives that service and withholds the worker’s payment, this too constitutes treachery and injustice.

I have discussed hiring someone to transport wine comprehensively in my book al-Sirāt al-Mustaqīm (The Straight Path). There I explained that the correct position is the one expressly stated by Ahmad: the worker should be awarded his payment, although it is not wholesome earnings for him; taking it is either discouraged or prohibited. This ruling, however, concerns work whose general category is permissible, such as transporting goods, unlike illicit sexual intercourse.

There is no doubt that a prostitute’s earnings are foul, as is a soothsayer’s fee. The judge orders the punishment of the hirer who has received the prohibited service, and the punishment imposed on him thus takes the place of the fee.

As for his responsibility before Allah, should he give the worker that payment, even though receiving it is unlawful on account of Allah’s right? This, then, has a compensable value. If he is not obliged to pay it, this would enable him to satisfy his desire: he commits the prohibited act and is excused, and Allah will not punish him in the Hereafter except

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man commissioned a book to be copied and gilded, paid the fee, received the book, bound it, and took it away for forty days. He then brought it back to the craftsman who had copied and gilded it and said, “Give me back the fee you received from me, for I am only an intermediary.” May he compel the craftsman to take it back and refund the fee he paid?

He replied:

If he hired him to perform work for which hiring is permissible, and paid him his fee upon completion of the work, the craftsman is not obliged to refund it. Indeed, if the intermediary did not name his principal in the hiring contract, he is undoubtedly liable for the fee.

If he did name his principal, is he still liable for the fee? There are two opinions, both reported from Imam Ahmad. Even if he had not paid the fee, the worker would have been entitled to demand it from him. What, then, if he has already paid it? Moreover, unless he paid the fee from his principal’s funds, the agent is entitled to recover from the principal the fee he paid on his behalf. And Allah knows best.

He cited as evidence the report that “the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, passed a shepherd while accompanied by Ibn ‘Abbās or someone else. He argued, “Had listening to the flute been forbidden, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would have instructed his companion to block his ears as he himself had done, or would have forbidden the shepherd to play.  وَفِي الْأَثَرِ:
 مَنْ شَهِدَ الْمَعْصِيَةَ وَكَرِهَهَا كَانَ كَمَنْ غَابَ عَنْهَا وَمَنْ غَابَ عَنْهَا وَرَضِيَهَا كَانَ كَمَنْ شَهِدَهَا. فَإِذَا شَهِدَهَا لِحَاجَةِ أَوْ لِإِكْرَاهِ أَنْكَرَهَا بِقَلْبِهِ؛ لِقَوْلِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{مَنْ رَأَى مِنْكُمْ مُنْكَرًا فَلْيُغَيِّرْهُ بِيَدِهِ. فَإِنْ لَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ فَبِلِسَانِهِ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ فَبِقَلْبِهِ وَذَلِكَ أَضْعَفُ الْإِيمَانِ}
 . فَلَوْ كَانَ الرَّجُلُ مَارًّا فَسَمِعَ الْقُرْآنَ مِنْ غَيْرِ أَنْ يَسْتَمِعَ إلَيْهِ لَمْ يُؤْجَرْ عَلَى ذَلِكَ؛
 وَإِنَّمَا يُؤْجَرُ عَلَى الِاسْتِمَاعِ الَّذِي يُقْصَدُ كَمَا قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَإِذَا قُرِئَ الْقُرْآنُ فَاسْتَمِعُوا لَهُ وَأَنْصِتُوا لَعَلَّكُمْ تُرْحَمُونَ}
 وَقَالَ لِمُوسَى: 
{فَاسْتَمِعْ لِمَا يُوحَى}
 .
translated_text:
along a road and hear such things; he incurs no sin thereby, by the agreement of the Muslims. But if he sits and deliberately listens without rejecting it in his heart, with his tongue, or with his hand, he is sinful, by the agreement of the Muslims. As Allah Most High says:

“When you see those who engage in mockery of Our revelations, turn away from them until they turn to another subject. And if Satan makes you forget, then once you remember, do not sit with the wrongdoing people. Those who fear Allah are in no way accountable for them, but should remind them, so that they may fear Him.”

Allah Most High also says:

“He has already revealed to you in the Book that when you hear Allah’s revelations being denied and mocked, you must not sit with them until they turn to another subject; otherwise, you would be like them.”

Thus, He places the person who sits and listens without rejecting it on the same footing as the perpetrator. Hence the saying: “The listener is a partner in the backbiter’s sin.” A report states:

“Whoever witnesses a sin and detests it is like one who was absent from it, and whoever is absent from it but approves of it is like one who witnessed it.”

If someone witnesses it because of a need or under compulsion, he must reject it in his heart, for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot, then with his tongue; and if he cannot, then with his heart—and that is the weakest level of faith.”

If a man were passing by and heard the Quran without deliberately listening to it, he would not be rewarded for that. Rather, he is rewarded for intentional listening, as Allah Most High says:

“When the Quran is recited, listen to it attentively and remain silent, so that you may receive mercy.”

And He said to Moses:

“So listen to what is revealed.”

فَإِذَا عُرِفَ أَنَّ الْأَمْرَ وَالنَّهْيَ وَالْوَعْدَ وَالْوَعِيدَ يَتَعَلَّقُ بِالِاسْتِمَاعِ؛

 أَنَّ زَمَّارَةَ الرَّاعِي لَيْسَتْ مُطْرِبَةً كالشبابة الَّتِي يَصْنَعُ غَيْرُ الرَّاعِي فَلَوْ قُدِّرَ الْإِذْنُ فِيهَا لَمْ يَلْزَمْ الْإِذْنُ فِي الْمَوْصُوفِ وَمَا يَتْبَعُهُ مِنْ الْأَصْوَاتِ الَّتِي تَفْعَلُ فِي النُّفُوسِ فِعْلَ حَمِيِّ الْكُؤُوسِ.
translated_text:
Once it is understood that commands, prohibitions, promises of reward, and threats of punishment concern deliberate listening, not merely hearing, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and Ibn ‘Umar were simply passing by, not deliberately listening. Likewise, Ibn ‘Umar, when accompanying the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and Nāfi‘, when accompanying Ibn ‘Umar, were merely hearing, not deliberately listening. Neither was therefore required to cover his ears.

The second point: The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, covered his ears only as an added precaution, so that he would not hear anything at all. This shows that avoiding hearing it is better than hearing it, even though merely hearing it entails no sin. Had the sound been permissible, he would not have covered his ears to avoid hearing something permissible. Rather, his covering his ears so as not to hear it—even though merely hearing it was not forbidden—indicates that refraining from deliberate listening is all the more appropriate. Thus, this provides stronger evidence for prohibiting deliberate listening than for permitting it.

The third point: Even assuming that deliberate listening is impermissible, if he and his companion had both covered their ears, they would not have known when the sound had ceased, so that the one being followed could uncover his ears.

The fourth point: It is not known whether the companion had reached puberty or was still a child below that age. Children are allowed forms of play that adults are not.

The fifth point: A shepherd’s pipe does not stir the emotions like the flute fashioned by someone other than a shepherd. Even if permission to hear it were assumed, this would not necessarily entail permission for what has been described and its accompanying sounds, which affect the soul as potent wine does.

" بِالْوَجْهِ السَّابِعِ "
: وَهُوَ أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ كُلُّ مَا جَازَ فِعْلُهُ جَازَ إعْطَاءُ الْعِوَضِ عَلَيْهِ.

{لَا سَبْقَ إلَّا فِي خُفٍّ أَوْ حَافِرٍ أَوْ نَصْلٍ}
 فَقَدْ نَهَى عَنْ السَّبْقِ فِي غَيْرِ هَذِهِ
translated_text:
The sixth point: Ibn al-Mundhir reported the scholars’ agreement on the prohibition of hiring people to sing or wail. He said:

“All the scholars whose views we have preserved agree that hiring female wailers and singers is invalid. Al-Sha‘bī, al-Nakha‘ī, and Mālik disapproved of it. Abū Thawr, al-Nu‘mān, Ya‘qūb, and Muhammad said: ‘Hiring anyone for any kind of singing or wailing is impermissible.’ This is also our position.”

Given that he reported the consensus of the scholars whose views he had preserved on the invalidity of hiring female wailers and singers—even though singing is permissible for women at weddings and on occasions of rejoicing, while for men it is either forbidden or disliked, though some scholars have allowed it—what, then, of the flute? None of the scholars permitted it for either men or women, whether at weddings or elsewhere. Those who permit it are not among the imams who are followed and renowned for their authority in religion.

Thus, the statement, “If one paid him for his flute-playing, that would be permissible,” is false and contrary to the positions of the imams of the Muslims, even if flute-playing were a permissible form of idle amusement. How much more so when it is a prohibited form of idle amusement! This becomes clear from the seventh point: not everything that is permissible to do may permissibly be done for payment.

Do you not see that, in the well-known hadith, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“No prize may be awarded except in camel racing, horse racing, or archery.”

He thus prohibited awarding prizes in competitions other than these

translated_text:
three activities. Yet wrestling may be permissible, as when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, wrestled Rukānah ibn ‘Abd Yazīd. Footracing is also permissible: the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, raced ‘Ā’ishah and permitted Salamah ibn al-Akwa‘ to race during the expedition of al-Ghābah and Dhū Qarad. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Every amusement a man engages in is vain, except shooting with his bow, training his horse, and playing with his wife, for these are worthwhile pursuits.”

Whoever takes money for such vain amusement takes it wrongfully. Nevertheless, this amusement may be permitted, just as children are permitted to play, and just as:

“Two young girls of the Ansār were singing during the days of Eid in ‘Ā’ishah’s house, while the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, neither listened to them nor forbade them. When Abū Bakr said, ‘Satan’s flute in the house of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him?’ the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said, ‘Leave them, Abū Bakr, for every people has a festival, and this is our festival.’”

He thereby showed that those for whom play is appropriate are permitted to play during festivals, even though men do not engage in such activities. But money must not be spent on vain amusement.

It is thus clear, on all these grounds, that anyone citing this hadith as evidence for the permissibility of that activity and of paying a fee for it would be mistaken even if the hadith were authentic. How much more so, then, given the defects it contains!

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—also said:

Section

When someone leases out land or properties such as houses, shops, inns, and the like, a binding lease binds both parties. It cannot bind one party while leaving the other free to terminate it. Rather, according to many scholars, it must either bind both parties or remain non-binding on both.

For example, if someone rents a property for one dirham per day without fixing an end date, this lease is non-binding according to one of the two scholarly opinions. For each day he occupies it, he becomes liable for that day’s rent. He may stay the following day, but the landlord may prevent him from doing so. The same applies if the rent is set at so much per month or per year without the two parties fixing an end date.

leave before the term expires, the landlord may not evict him before its expiry, whether because he receives a higher offer during the term or for any other reason. This applies whether the property is an endowment or unrestricted private property, and whether it belongs to an orphan or anyone else. This is the position of the four imams and other leading Muslim scholars. None of the imams held that an unqualified lease could bind the tenant without binding the landlord, whether it concerns an endowment, an orphan’s property, or anything else. Even if a later scholar departs from this and reports disagreement over some aspect of it, the imams’ agreement predates him.

Allah Most High has commanded the fulfilment of contracts and covenants. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“On the Day of Resurrection, a banner will be raised by the backside of every betrayer, proportionate to his betrayal.”

He also said:

“Whoever possesses four traits is a complete hypocrite, and whoever possesses one of them has a trait of hypocrisy until he abandons it: when he speaks, he lies; when entrusted, he betrays the trust; when he makes a covenant, he breaks it; and when he disputes, he transgresses all bounds.”

If the administrator tells the prospective tenant, “I will draw up a lease for you; take up residence,” he has thereby leased the property to him. If he has not leased it to him, he is not permitted to hand the property over to him, for he would then have handed over the endowment and the orphan’s property in an impermissible manner, thereby committing a wrong and incurring liability.

If the occupant had not rented the property, he would be entitled to leave whenever he wished, and he would be a usurper. He would not owe the stipulated rent, but rather the fair rental value of the use he had enjoyed, according to one of the two scholarly opinions. According to those who hold that no compensation is owed for the use of usurped property, no compensation would be due

At most, it might be said that he took possession of it under an invalid lease. Were that so, he would be entitled to leave whenever he wished; indeed, he would be obliged to return the property to the landlord, as with anything received under an invalid contract. Moreover, according to one of the two scholarly opinions, he would owe the stipulated rent or the fair rental value. According to the other, he would owe whichever of the two is less.

Thus, a higher offer may not be accepted, whether the property is an endowment, an orphan’s property, or anything else, unless the lease is nonbinding. This is the case when the tenant is free to leave and hand the property back to them whenever he wishes—what people commonly call “vacating and locking up.” If he is free to vacate and lock up, the landlord is likewise free to evict him and lease the property to someone else, even if no higher offer has been made. He must act according to what he judges to be in the best interests.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

Is it permissible to lease orchards and land containing date palms or other trees before their fruit has begun to ripen, for one or two years, or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah.

There are three opinions on this issue.

The first is that this is impermissible under all circumstances, on the grounds that it falls within the Messenger of Allah’s prohibition—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—against selling fruit before it has begun to ripen. It is therefore impermissible, just as it is outside such a lease: for example, purchasing the fruit alone after it has appeared but before it has begun to ripen, with the seller bearing the expense of watering and tending it until it is fully ripe.

This is the well-known position in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, and it is transmitted as an explicit ruling of Ahmad. Abū Hanīfah’s position on this is even more restrictive.

The proponents of this opinion disagree over whether it is permissible to circumvent this prohibition by leasing out the land and entering into a tree-tending contract stipulating a very small share of the fruit. They hold two opinions. Ahmad’s explicit ruling is that this is impermissible. Al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā stated in his book Ibtāl al-hiyal (Invalidating Legal Stratagems):

that it is permissible. This is the recognized position among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī.

Yet this stratagem is unworkable even on the principles of those who uphold the validity of legal stratagems. It is invalid on several grounds:

One is that, among the many properties concerned, some are endowments or belong to an orphan or someone else whose assets are administered under legal guardianship. Entering into a tree-tending contract for such property in return for a very small share of its fruit is impermissible, and making either contract conditional upon the other is invalid.

Another is that the harm underlying the prohibition against selling fruit before it has begun to ripen—such as its involving uncertainty akin to gambling, and its leading to disputes and enmity, among the very harms for which gambling was prohibited—is present in these transactions to an even greater extent than in the simple sale of fruit before it has begun to ripen. It is well known that the party undertaking such an arrangement pays his money only in return for the benefit he will derive from the land and trees, especially where the benefit from the trees predominates, as in gardens and orchards mostly occupied by trees or containing little open ground. Here, if Allah withholds the fruit and the party liable for the rent is required to pay it in full, the resulting wrongful consumption of wealth, disputes, and evil are plain to see.

Another is that renting for a thousand dirhams land whose rental value is one hundred dirhams is the conduct of financially irresponsible people who deserve to be placed under legal interdiction. The same applies to a tree-tending contract for a share

of one thousandth for their owner—another act of financial irresponsibility warranting legal interdiction. Whoever does this must be placed under legal interdiction by the authorities, rather than having the contract enforced and declared valid.

If it is argued, “He may grant a concession under this contract because of the concession he receives from the other party under the other contract,” the answer is: “If he is entitled to that reciprocal concession, then one of the two contracts must be a condition of the other. If he is not entitled to it, then he is granting a concession under this contract without a corresponding concession from the other party under that contract.”

Such an arrangement is beneficial only when both parties take possession of what they are to receive. If a man grants someone a concession on one commodity, and the other grants him a concession on another, and both take possession, it might be said that the intended purpose is thereby achieved, whether in a case like this or in a case like this. Yet the fruit may or may not materialize, while the other party is entitled to demand the full rent even if no fruit materializes. This is not financially sound conduct; rather, it is the conduct of financially irresponsible people who deserve to be placed under legal interdiction.

This is especially so if the person administering the property has no authority to make gratuitous concessions, such as an administrator of an endowment or an orphan’s property. He would say to the tenant, “I am obliged to demand the full rent from you, whether or not the fruit materializes.” Would a financially responsible person enter into such an arrangement, paying a thousand dirhams for the use of land whose rental value is a hundred dirhams, hoping that the fruit will be delivered to him and come into his possession, while remaining liable for the rent whether or not the fruit materializes? If he did so, would this be anything other than engaging in the very thing the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited?

translated_text:
For in the two Sahīh collections, Ibn ‘Umar reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“forbade selling fruit before its soundness became apparent, forbidding both seller and buyer.”

If this tenant pays his money to obtain the fruit, then, according to their own position, he is effectively the purchaser whom the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited from doing so. How, then, can he pay his money for such a transaction? There is abundant evidence that transactions of this kind are invalid, which we have discussed elsewhere. A jurist is not someone who takes a practice that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited to avert harm to people, only to turn instead to something even more harmful. Such a person is like someone seeking refuge from scorching ground in a fire.

This can be understood from the principle of invalidating legal stratagems: many of them entail greater corruption and harm than openly committing the prohibited act. As Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī said:

“They seek to deceive Allah as though they were deceiving children. It would be less objectionable to me if they did it straightforwardly.”

For this reason, tahlīl marriage—a marriage intended to make a divorced woman lawful again for her former husband—entails greater corruption than temporary marriage. A man entering a temporary marriage intends to be married for a certain period, whereas a man entering a tahlīl marriage has no such purpose. Every harm underlying the prohibition of temporary marriage is therefore present in tahlīl marriage, with further harms besides. This is why people’s hearts recoil more strongly from tahlīl marriage than from temporary marriage. Temporary marriage was permitted in the early days of Islam

and the early Muslims disputed whether it remained lawful. Marriage for the purpose of tahlīl, however, was never permitted, nor did the early Muslims dispute its prohibition. The second view on the original question is that, if the use of the land is the principal object and the trees are incidental, the land may be leased with the trees included incidentally. This is Mālik’s position, and he sets the incidental portion at one-third. Someone holding this view permits the sale of fruit before its soundness becomes apparent when it is included incidentally within another transaction. Similarly, in a purchase made after pollination, the purchaser may stipulate that the fruit be included, as is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the two Sahīh collections. Here, the purchaser has bought the fruit before its soundness becomes apparent, but only as an adjunct to the principal property. This is permissible by scholarly consensus. Thus, he draws an analogy between what is included incidentally in a lease and what is included incidentally in a sale.

translated_text:
the Faithful, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb. He leased out the orchard of Usayd ibn Hudayr for three years, received the rent, and used it to settle Usayd’s debt. This was related by Harb al-Kirmānī, a companion of Imam Ahmad, in his well-known collection of questions answered by Ahmad. It was also related by Abū Zur‘a al-Dimashqī and others, and is well known as an action of ‘Umar. Trees predominate in the orchards of Medina.

One of the Zāhirī jurists of the Maghreb mentioned this report from ‘Umar in his writings and claimed that it contradicted scholarly consensus. This claim has no substance; indeed, a claim of consensus permitting it would be more plausible. ‘Umar did this in the Prophet’s city, in the presence of the Emigrants and the Helpers. This was a matter likely to become widely known, yet no objection to it has been reported from anyone. They would object to lesser matters, even when ‘Umar himself did them, just as ‘Imrān ibn Husayn and others objected to his stance on combining ‘umrah with Hajj. This case is comparable to ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān’s ruling that the wife of ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf should inherit from him, although he had irrevocably divorced her during his final illness, and to similar cases. What ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb did was correct.

When a jurist reflects on the foundational principles of the Sharia, it becomes clear to him that property of this kind does not fall within the scope of what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited. This becomes evident in several ways:

First, it is well known that land can be leased, and that the grain growing on it can be sold before it hardens. Yet when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited selling grain before it hardens, this did not constitute a prohibition on leasing land

even though the tenant’s objective is the grain. For it is the tenant who works the land until he obtains the grain, unlike the purchaser, who buys only the grain, while the seller remains responsible for tending it until it is ready. Likewise, the Prophet’s prohibition on selling grapes before they turn dark does not prohibit someone from taking trees under a lease, tending them and watering them until they bear fruit. Rather, the prohibition concerns someone who purchases only the grapes, while the seller remains responsible for tending them until they fully ripen, as happens when people purchase grapes from what are known as vineyards. For this reason, these people do not sell them until their ripeness becomes apparent, unlike the practice of leasing the trees.

Second:

Sharecropping on land is comparable to tending trees in return for a share of their fruit. Both are permissible according to the hadith jurists, such as Imam Ahmad and others, including Ibn Khuzayma and Ibn al-Mundhir. Sharecropping is also permissible according to Ibn Abī Laylā, Abū Yūsuf, Muhammad, al-Layth ibn Sa‘d and other imams. Its permissibility is established by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the consensus of his Companions after him.

Those who prohibited it thought that it fell under leasing and would therefore constitute a lease for an unspecified consideration, which is impermissible. Abū Hanīfa applied his analogy consistently and did not permit it under any circumstances. Al-Shāfi‘ī, however, made an exception where there was a need, as when open land is included incidentally with the trees in an agreement to tend them for a share of their fruit. Mālik did likewise, though, in accordance with his principles, account is taken of whether the amount of such land is small or large. translated_text:
hiring for an unspecified consideration, and that it was permitted out of necessity, since the owner of the money cannot lease it out.

The correct understanding is that these transactions are partnerships. Sharecropping is a partnership: one party contributes the use of his labour, and the other the use of his property. Whatever profit Allah apportions is shared between them, as between partners in an ‘inān partnership. Thus, the work itself is neither the object of the contract nor specified as it is in a contract of hire. If this were a contract of hire, the work would have to be specified.

To describe it as a reward-based contract would be closer, since the work in such a contract need not be specified. Moreover, it is a revocable, non-binding contract. Yet it is not a reward-based contract either, because in such a contract the two parties seek different kinds of things: one seeks the return of his runaway slave or the construction of his wall, while the other seeks the stipulated reward. In agreements to tend trees for a share of their fruit, sharecropping agreements, and profit-sharing investments, however, both parties seek the same kind of thing: profit. They share alike in gain and loss: if one receives something, so does the other; and if one receives nothing, neither does the other.

For this reason, what is stipulated for either party must be an undivided share of the profit, of the same kind as that stipulated for the other; it cannot be a specified fixed amount. This establishes that these transactions are partnerships, like an ‘inān partnership, in which the two parties share in the profit. If a fixed sum were stipulated, whether from the profit or otherwise, that would not be permissible. This is the form of sharecropping that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited, as related

 كَانَ اللَّيْثِ أَفْقَهَ مِنْ مَالِكٍ. فَإِنَّهُ بَيَّنَ أَنَّ الَّذِي نَهَى عَنْهُ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مُوَافِقٌ لِقِيَاسِ الْأُصُولِ؛ لِمَا فِيهِ مِنْ أَنْ يُشْتَرَطَ لِأَحَدِ الشَّرِيكَيْنِ شَيْءٌ مُعَيَّنٌ مِنْ الرِّبْحِ. وَالشَّرِكَةُ حَقُّهَا الْعَدْلُ بَيْنَ الشَّرِيكَيْنِ فِيمَا لَهُمَا مِنْ الْمَغْنَمِ وَعَلَيْهِمَا مِنْ الْمَغْرَمِ. فَإِذَا خَرَجَتْ كَانَ ظُلْمًا مُحَرَّمًا. وَأَيْنَ مَنْ يَجْعَلُ مَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ السُّنَّةُ مُوَافِقًا لِلْأُصُولِ إلَى مَنْ يَجْعَلُ مَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ السُّنَّةُ مُخَالِفًا لِلْأُصُولِ.
 وَمَنْ أَعْطَى النَّظَرَ حَقَّهُ عَلِمَ أَنَّ مَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ السُّنَّةُ مِنْ النَّهْيِ عَنْ هَذِهِ الْمُخَابَرَةِ وَمِنْ مُعَامَلَةِ أَهْلِ خَيْبَرَ بِشَطْرِ مَا يَخْرُجُ مِنْهَا مِنْ ثَمَرٍ وَزَرْعٍ بِدُونِ هَذَا الشَّرْطِ وَمَا عَمِلَ بِهِ الصَّحَابَةُ مِنْ الْمُضَارَبَةِ:
 كُلُّ ذَلِكَ عَلَى وَفْقِ الْقِيَاسِ. وَأَنَّ هَذَا مِنْ جِنْسِ الْمُشَارَكَاتِ لَا مِنْ جِنْسِ الْمُؤَجَّرَاتِ.
 وَإِذَا كَانَ كَذَلِكَ فَنَقُولُ:
 مَعْلُومٌ أَنَّهُ إذَا سَاقَاهُ عَلَى الشَّجَرِ بِجُزْءِ مِنْ الثَّمَرَةِ كَانَ كَمَا إذَا زَارَعَهُ
translated_text:
in detail in Sahīh Muslim and elsewhere, on the authority of Rāfi‘ ibn Khadīj: they used to lease out land, stipulating that the landowner would receive the crops from a particular plot, such as those growing along large waterways and irrigation channels. Sometimes the crops in one area would survive while those in another would not.

For this reason, al-Layth ibn Sa‘d said:
“The form of sharecropping that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited is something that anyone knowledgeable about the lawful and unlawful would, upon examining it, recognize as impermissible.”

This reflects the juristic understanding of al-Layth, of whom al-Shāfi‘ī said:
“Al-Layth had a deeper understanding of jurisprudence than Mālik.”

For he explained that what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited accords with analogical reasoning from established principles, since it involves stipulating a particular portion of the profit for one of the two partners. A partnership requires fairness between the partners in the gains they receive and the losses they bear. If it departs from this, it becomes an unlawful injustice. What a difference there is between someone who regards what the Sunnah teaches as consistent with established principles and someone who regards it as contrary to them!

Anyone who gives the matter due consideration will recognize that the Sunnah’s prohibition of this form of sharecropping, its account of the agreement with the people of Khaybar for half of the fruit and crops produced there without this stipulation, and the Companions’ practice of profit-sharing investment all accord with analogical reasoning. These transactions belong to the category of partnerships, not contracts of hire.

That being so, we say: it is well known that if someone contracts with another to tend trees in return for a share of their fruit, this is like entering into a sharecropping agreement with him

عَلَى الْأَرْضِ بِجُزْءِ مِنْ الزَّرْعِ وَضَارَبَهُ عَلَى النَّقْدِ بِجُزْءِ مِنْ الرِّبْحِ فَقَدْ جُعِلَتْ الثَّمَرَةُ مِنْ بَابِ النَّمَاءِ وَالْفَائِدَةُ الْحَاصِلَةُ بِبَدَنِ هَذَا وَمَالِ هَذَا. وَاَلَّذِي نَهَى عَنْهُ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مِنْ بَيْعِ الثَّمَرَةِ لَيْسَ لِلْمُشْتَرِي عَمَلٌ فِي حُصُولِهِ أَصْلًا؛ بَلْ الْعَمَلُ كُلُّهُ عَلَى الْبَائِعِ فَإِذَا اسْتَأْجَرَ الْأَرْضَ وَالشَّجَرَ حَتَّى حَصَلَ لَهُ ثَمَرٌ وَزَرْعٌ. كَانَ كَمَا إذَا اسْتَأْجَرَ الْأَرْضَ حَتَّى يَحْصُلَ لَهُ الزَّرْعُ.

 فَإِنْ قِيلَ:
 إنَّ هَذَا يَقْتَضِي أَنَّ الْأَعْيَانَ مَعْقُودٌ عَلَيْهَا فِي الْإِجَارَةِ وَالْإِجَارَةُ إنَّمَا هِيَ عَقْدٌ عَلَى الْمَنَافِعِ لَا عَلَى الْأَعْيَانِ وَإِنَّمَا جَازَتْ إجَارَةُ الظِّئْرِ عَلَى خِلَافِ الْقِيَاسِ.
 قِيلَ:
 الْجَوَابُ مِنْ وَجْهَيْنِ.
translated_text:
on land for a share of its crops, or entrusting him with money for a share of the profit. The fruit is thus treated as growth and gain produced by one party’s labour and the other’s property. In the sale of fruit prohibited by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, however, the buyer does no work at all to produce it; rather, all the work falls to the seller. Thus, leasing land and trees to obtain fruit and crops is like leasing land to obtain crops.

The third point:

Fruit is treated like benefits and yields in endowments, loans for use, and similar arrangements. Trees may therefore be endowed so that the beneficiaries of the endowment benefit from their fruit, just as land may be endowed so that they benefit from its yield. It is also permissible to grant someone the fruit of trees, just as it is permissible to lend a mount for riding, lend a house for use, or lend a milk-producing animal for its milk.

All these arrangements involve gratuitously granting the growth and benefit of property. Giving someone a property to live in is like giving him an animal to ride, trees whose fruit he may harvest, land to cultivate, or a she-camel or ewe whose milk he may drink. These benefits may be the subject of gratuitous contracts, whether the underlying asset is rendered inalienable, as in an endowment, or not. They may also be the subject of partnership contracts; likewise, they may be the subject of contracts involving an exchange for consideration.

If it is objected:

“This entails making tangible assets the subject of a lease, whereas a lease is a contract for benefits, not tangible assets. Hiring a wet nurse is permitted only as an exception to analogical reasoning.”

The reply is:

There are two answers.

original_text:

 فَإِنْ قِيلَ:
 فَهَذَا يَقْتَضِي جَوَازَ إجَارَةِ الْحَيَوَانِ لِشُرْبِ لَبَنِهِ.
 قِيلَ:
 وَفِي هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ نِزَاعٌ بَيْنَ الْفُقَهَاءِ أَيْضًا. وَالْمُزَارَعَةُ إنَّمَا تَكُونُ بِدَلِيلِ
translated_text:
The first answer:

Leasing land and trees is not a contract for a tangible asset. Rather, it is comparable to leasing land for cultivation. The tangible produce is what the tenant seeks, since he leases the land only to obtain crops; nevertheless, the contract concerns benefits, which are analogous to these tangible yields.

The second answer:

We do not concede that hiring a wet nurse is contrary to analogical reasoning. How could this be said when the only hiring expressly mentioned in the Quran as part of our law is the hiring of a wet nurse, in the words of Allah Most High:

“If they breastfeed for you, give them their payment.”

Those who considered this contrary to analogical reasoning did so only because they mistakenly assumed that a lease could concern benefits alone. That is not the case. Rather, a lease may concern anything that can be obtained while its underlying source remains intact, whether tangible produce or a benefit.

Since a wet nurse’s milk can be obtained while its source remains intact, as can the water accumulated in a well, these may be the subject of a lease just as benefits may. Allah brings these tangible yields into existence successively while their source remains intact, just as He brings benefits into existence successively while their source remains intact. Hence, these underlying assets may be endowed with these yields—both tangible produce and benefits—reserved.

If it is objected:

“This would entail permitting the leasing of an animal in order to drink its milk.”

The reply is:

This question, too, is disputed among the jurists. Crop-sharing can only be justified by evidence

translated_text:
grounded in Islamic law—a scriptural text, consensus, analogical reasoning, or the like. As for disputed cases raised as objections, we give a general answer:

If the evidence we have cited establishes the validity of this lease, that evidence must be applied consistently and acted upon. If it does not establish its validity, this constitutes no flaw in our argument.

As for the evidence said to invalidate this lease, if it can be reconciled with the evidence already mentioned, there is no contradiction. Otherwise, the evidence we have cited carries greater weight, for prohibiting benefits rests only on the same kind of grounds invoked in the disputed case here.

If it is objected:

“Ibn ʿAqīl permitted leasing land and trees together because of need, following Mālik’s approach. However, Mālik stipulated that the trees be few, whereas Ibn ʿAqīl imposed no such restriction. There is a need to lease open land containing trees, and leasing the land separately from the trees is impossible or difficult because of the harm this entails. He therefore permitted the trees to be included in the lease, just as al-Shāfiʿī permitted land to be included incidentally with trees in contracts to tend trees for a share of their fruit.

“Part of Ibn ʿAqīl’s argument is that this amounts, at most, to permitting fruit to be sold before its ripeness becomes apparent, as an adjunct to something else, because of need. Scriptural evidence and consensus permit this when someone sells trees bearing fruit that has already appeared, with the purchaser stipulating that the fruit be included. The purchaser has thus bought both trees and fruit before the fruit’s ripeness becomes apparent. Yet what you have stated implies that permitting this accords with analogical reasoning, and that it is permissible without such need, even when the trees are leased on their own.”

قِيلَ:
 هَذَا زِيَادَةُ تَوْكِيدٍ؛
 فَإِنَّ هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةَ لَهَا مَأْخَذَانِ أَحَدُهُمَا:
 أَنْ يُسَلِّمَ أَنَّ الْأَصْلَ يَقْتَضِي الْمَنْعَ لَكِنْ يَجُوزُ ذَلِكَ لِأَجْلِ الْحَاجَةِ. كَمَا فِي نَظَائِرِهِ.
 وَالثَّانِي:
 أَنْ يَمْنَعَ هَذَا وَيُقَالَ: لَا نُسَلِّمُ أَنَّ الْأَصْلَ يَقْتَضِي الْمَنْعَ؛ بَلْ الدَّلِيلُ لَا يَتَنَاوَلُ مِثْلَ هَذِهِ الصُّورَةِ؛ لَا لَفْظًا وَلَا مَعْنًى.
 أَمَّا لَفْظًا فَإِنَّ هَذَا لَمْ يَبِعْ ثَمَرَةً قَبْلَ بُدُوِّ صَلَاحِهَا وَلَوْ كَانَ قَدْ بَاعَ لَكَانَ عَلَيْهِ مُؤْنَةُ التَّوْفِيَةِ كَمَا لَوْ بَاعَهَا بَعْدَ بُدُوِّ صَلَاحِهَا فَإِنَّ مُؤْنَةَ التَّوْفِيَةِ عَلَيْهِ أَيْضًا فَإِنَّ الْمُسْلِمِينَ اتَّفَقُوا عَلَى مَا فَعَلَهُ أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ مِنْ ضَرْبِ الْخَرَاجِ عَلَى السَّوَادِ وَغَيْرِهِ مِنْ الْأَرْضِ الَّتِي فُتِحَتْ عَنْوَةً سَوَاءٌ قِيلَ:
 إنَّهُ يَجِبُ فِي الْأَرْضِ الَّتِي فُتِحَتْ عَنْوَةً أَوْ تُجْعَلَ فَيْئًا كَمَا قَالَهُ مَالِكٍ وَهُوَ رِوَايَةٌ عَنْ أَحْمَدَ.
 أَوْ قِيلَ:
 إنَّهُ يَجِبُ قِسْمَتُهَا بَيْنَ الْغَانِمِينَ كَمَا قَالَهُ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَهُوَ رِوَايَةٌ عَنْ الْإِمَامِ.
 أَوْ قِيلَ:
 يُخَيَّرُ الْإِمَامُ فِيهَا بَيْنَ هَذَا وَهَذَا كَمَا هُوَ مَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَالثَّوْرِيِّ وَأَبِي عُبَيْدٍ وَنَحْوِهِمْ. وَهُوَ ظَاهِرُ مَذْهَبِ الْإِمَامِ أَحْمَدَ.
 فَإِنَّ الشَّافِعِيِّ يَقُولُ:
 إنَّ عُمَرَ اسْتَطَابَ أَنْفُسَ الْغَانِمِينَ حَتَّى جَعَلَهَا فَيْئًا وَضَرَبَ الْخَرَاجَ عَلَيْهَا فَاتَّفَقَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ فِي الْجُمْلَةِ عَلَى أَنَّ وَضْعَ الْخَرَاجِ عَلَى أَرْضِ الْعَنْوَةِ جَائِزٌ إذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ فِيهِ ظُلْمٌ لِلْغَانِمَيْنِ.
translated_text:
The reply is:

This provides further confirmation, for this question may be approached on two grounds. The first is to concede that the basic principle entails prohibition, but that need makes it permissible, as in comparable cases.

The second is to reject this premise and say: “We do not concede that the basic principle entails prohibition. Rather, the evidence does not cover a case such as this, either in its wording or in its underlying meaning.”

As for its wording, this person has not sold fruit before its ripeness becomes apparent. Had he sold it, he would have borne the costs of delivery, just as he would also bear those costs if he sold it after its ripeness became apparent.

The Muslims have agreed upon what the Commander of the Faithful, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—did in imposing kharāj (land tax) on the Sawād and other lands conquered by force. This holds whether the position taken is that this is obligatory on land conquered by force, or that the land should be made communal property, as Mālik held—which is also one reported view of Ahmad—or that it must be divided among those who took part in the conquest, as al-Shāfi‘ī held—which is also one reported view of the Imam—or that the ruler may choose between these two alternatives, as held by Abū Hanīfah, al-Thawrī, Abū ‘Ubayd, and others. This last position is also the apparent position of Imam Ahmad’s school.

Al-Shāfi‘ī maintains that ‘Umar obtained the willing consent of those who took part in the conquest before making the land communal property and imposing kharāj upon it. Thus, the Muslims have agreed in general that imposing kharāj on land conquered by force is permissible, provided that it entails no injustice to those who took part in the conquest.

ثُمَّ الْخَرَاجُ عِنْدَ أَكْثَرِهِمْ أُجْرَةُ الْأَرْضِ وَأَنَّهُ لَمْ يَقْدِرْ مُدَّةَ الْإِجَارَةِ لِعُمُومِ مَصْلَحَتِهَا وَالْخَرَاجُ ضَرِيبَةٌ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ الَّتِي فِيهَا شَجَرٌ وَالْأَرْضِ الْبَيْضَاءِ. وَضَرَبَ عَلَى جَرِيبِ النَّخْلِ مِقْدَارًا وَعَلَى جَرِيبِ الْكَرْمِ مِقْدَارًا. وَهَذَا بِعَيْنِهِ إجَارَةٌ لِلْأَرْضِ مَعَ الشَّجَرِ؛ فَإِنْ كَانَ جَوَازُ هَذَا عَلَى وَفْقِ الْقِيَاسِ فَهُوَ الْمَطْلُوبُ. وَإِنْ كَانَ جَوَازُ ذَلِكَ لِحَاجَةِ دَاعِيَةٍ إلَى ذَلِكَ؛
 فَإِنَّ النَّاسَ لَهُمْ بَسَاتِينُ فِيهَا مَسَاكِنُ وَلَهَا أُجُورٌ وَافِرَةٌ فَإِنْ دَفَعُوهَا إلَى مَنْ يَعْمَلُهَا مُسَاقَاةً وَمُزَارَعَةً:
 تَعَطَّلَتْ مَنْفَعَةُ الْمَسَاكِنِ عَلَيْهَا كَمَا فِي أَرْضِ دِمَشْقَ وَنَحْوِهَا. ثُمَّ قَدْ يَكُونُ وَقْفًا أَوْ لِيَتِيمِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ. فَكَيْفَ يَجُوزُ تَعْطِيلُ مَنْفَعَةِ الْمَسْكَنِ الْمَبْنِيَّةِ فِي تِلْكَ الْحَدَائِقِ. وَقَدْ تَكُونُ مَنْفَعَةُ الْمَسْكَنِ هِيَ أَكْثَرُ الْمَنْفَعَةِ وَمَنْفَعَةُ الشَّجَرِ وَالْأَرْضِ تَابِعَةً فَيَحْتَاجُونَ إلَى إجَارَةِ تِلْكَ الْمَسَاكِنِ وَلَا يُمْكِنُ أَنْ تُؤَجَّرَ دُونَ مَنْفَعَةِ الْأَرْضِ وَالشَّجَرِ؛
 فَإِنَّ الْعَامِلَ إذَا كَانَ غَيْرَ السَّاكِنِ تَضَرَّرَ هَذَا وَهَذَا تَضَرَّرَ:
 بِبِنَاءِ الْمَسَاكِنِ وَيَبْقَى مَمْنُوعًا مِنْ الِانْتِفَاعِ بِالثَّمَرِ وَالزَّرْعِ هُوَ وَعِيَالُهُ مَعَ كَوْنِهِ عِنْدَهُمْ وَيَتَضَرَّرُونَ بِدُخُولِ الْعَامِلِ عَلَيْهِمْ فِي دَارِهِمْ وَالْعَامِلُ أَيْضًا لَا يَبْقَى مُطْمَئِنًّا إلَى سَلَامَةِ ثَمَرِهِ وَزَرْعِهِ؛ بَلْ يَخَافُ عَلَيْهَا فِي مَغِيبِهِ. وَمَا كَلُّ سَاكِنٍ أَمِينًا وَلَوْ كَانَ أَمِينًا لَمْ تُؤْمَنْ الضِّيفَانُ وَالصِّبْيَانُ والنسوان. وَكُلُّ هَذَا مَعْلُومٌ. فَإِذَا كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ نَهَى عَنْ الْمُزَابَنَةِ وَهِيَ بَيْعُ
translated_text:
Moreover, according to most of them, kharāj is rent for the land, and ‘Umar did not fix the duration of the lease because of the general benefit it served. Kharāj is a levy on both land bearing trees and treeless land. He imposed a specified amount on each jarīb (a unit of land area) of date palms, and a specified amount on each jarīb of vines. This is precisely a lease of land together with its trees. If permitting this accords with legal analogy, that establishes our point. If, however, it is permitted because of a compelling need, then people own orchards containing dwellings that command substantial rents. If they entrust these properties to someone to cultivate under fruit-sharing and crop-sharing agreements, the benefit of the dwellings on them is lost, as happens in the countryside around Damascus and similar places.

Furthermore, the property may be an endowment, belong to an orphan, or the like. How, then, can it be permissible to forgo the benefit of the dwellings built in those gardens? The dwelling may provide most of the benefit, with the trees and land being merely ancillary. They therefore need to lease those dwellings, yet cannot lease them separately from the use of the land and trees.

For if the cultivator is someone other than the resident, both suffer harm: there is harm from the construction of the dwellings, and the resident and his dependants remain barred from benefiting from the fruit and crops, despite their being right there with them. They are also inconvenienced by the cultivator entering their home. The cultivator, too, cannot remain confident that his fruit and crops are safe; rather, he fears for them during his absence. Not every resident is trustworthy, and even if he is trustworthy, his guests, children, and womenfolk cannot be relied upon. All this is well known.

translated_text:
fresh dates for dried dates, because this involves exchanging an item subject to the rules of ribā for another of the same kind without measuring their quantities—and the prohibitions concerning ribā are stricter than those concerning gambling—yet he permitted ‘arāyā sales on the basis of estimated yields because of need, and instructed a man to sell a tree he owned on another person’s property, or give it to him, because the property owner suffered harm from the man entering his property. When he did neither, the Prophet ordered the tree to be uprooted. Thus he required a transfer for compensation to remove the harm suffered by the property owner, just as he established a co-owner’s right to acquire a share at its sale price to avert the harm arising from co-ownership and partition. How much more so, then, when the harm is as described!

It is well known that the Sharia came to secure and perfect benefits, and to eliminate and reduce harms. We have been commanded to give precedence to the greater of two benefits by forgoing the lesser, and to avert the greater of two evils by tolerating the lesser. The harm in this situation is greater than the harm we previously mentioned as possibly affecting one of the parties to the exchange. Here, the harm is considerable and certain; there, if any harm occurs, it is slight and doubtful.

Moreover, fruit-sharing and crop-sharing agreements depend on the cultivator’s trustworthiness, which may often be difficult to find. People therefore need leasing arrangements, under which payment is a binding debt. For this reason, many people in many places and times turn from crop-sharing to leasing.

It is well known that the Sharia imposes obligations according to what is possible, and likewise stipulates conditions for acts of worship and contracts according to what is possible. Thus, despite a ruler’s sinfulness, legal effect may still be given to such of his acts of governance and distribution

and adjudication as are permissible, although a ruler must be upright whenever this is possible without causing a greater harm. The same applies to prayer leaders when it is only possible to pray behind a sinful person.

Thus, if land can only be handed over to a sinful person, and entrusting him with it would lead to harm, it becomes necessary to lease it to him. This is one ground for permitting leasing. Moreover, there may be no one available to take it under a sharing arrangement, such as fruit-sharing or crop-sharing. Unless it is leased out, it will lie unused and its owners will suffer harm, even if they are poor. The only harm involved here is the possibility that the fruit yield may fall below its usual level, leaving an element of risk.

This degree of risk can be offset by providing the lessee with compensation. Likewise, in a lawful lease, if the benefit is lost, the corresponding rent is no longer due. The same applies, according to the correct view, if the benefit is diminished: the rent is reduced in proportion to that diminution. It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) ordered that payment be remitted for produce struck by calamities, and said:

“If you sell something to your brother and it is struck by a calamity, it is not lawful for you to take any of your brother’s money. On what grounds would any of you take his brother’s money without right?”

This is the position of Mālik, Ahmad and others. This is because, although the fruit has been taken into possession, possession is not yet complete in a way that enables its recipient to harvest it.
